You reported a power analysis that has been classified as 'post-hoc'. Calculating observed power is [almost never useful](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/08-samplesizejustification.html#sec-posthocpower). If you actually performed a sensitivity power analysis, label it as such explicitly.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Cannabis use disorder (CUD) frequently co-occurs with depressive symptoms, yet shared underlying neurobiological mechanisms remain unclear.

This study invesAgated the role of depressive symptoms in the relaAonship between CUD, cannabis use characterisAcs, and within-network resAngstate funcAonal connecAvity (RSFC) in the ExecuAve Control (ECN), the Salience (SN), the Default Mode (DMN), and the Basal Ganglia (BGN) networks.
Methods: In a pooled sample of 132 CUD parAcipants and 102 controls, we examined the associaAons of group, depressive symptoms, and their interacAon with within-network RSFC.
Within the CUD group, we assessed the associaAons between cannabis use characterisAcs, depressive symptoms, and RSFC.
We also conducted an exploratory, non-preregistered sensiAvity analysis in the largest contribuAng study (n = 187).

Results: In the full sample and the largest study, depressive symptoms were associated with higher RSFC in the leU ECN and interacted with group in the right ECN, showing a posiAve associaAon between depressive symptoms and RECN RSFC in controls, but not in CUD individuals.
The largest study analysis addiAonally showed lower dorsal SN and higher BGN RSFC in CUD individuals relaAve to controls.
Within the full CUD sample, depressive symptoms were posiAvely associated with anterior SN RSFC among individuals with heavier cannabis use, but negaAvely among those with lighter use.
Conclusion: CUD, heaviness of cannabis use, and depressive symptoms may concurrently relate to RSFC alteraAons within disAnct networks.
Group differences potenAally emerge at higher levels of CUD and depression severity.
This highlights the importance of accounAng for depressive symptoms in neurobiological research on CUD.

Cannabis use (CU) and cannabis use disorder (CUD) are prevalent worldwide and are oUen accompanied by psychiatric comorbidiAes, including depressive symptoms of varying severity (Hasin and Walsh, 2020; Onaemo et al., 2021).
